title: How much is in the account after the next day's deposit?
description: A bank account opens with one hundred rupees, and sixty rupees are put in the next day. The money put in is a credit, and it is added to the balance. Keeko ties the credit to the plus press of the lift attendant in the book.
teaching_notes: One idea: a credit is money put into the account, so it is a positive number added to the balance. Watch for students who forget what the starting balance was.

source: You open a bank account with the ₹100 you saved. Then you make ₹60 at your job the next day and you deposit it in your account (a 'credit').
video_script.why: The child adds a credit to the opening bank balance and sees a credit as a positive number.
video_script.substitution: Write the credit as a positive number and add it to the balance.
video_script.payoff_line: The new balance is one hundred and sixty rupees.
maths_rules: a credit of ₹60 is money put in: +60
video_script.design: One idea: a credit is a positive number and it is added to the balance. A passbook page shows the opening balance and the next day's credit. Keeko ties the credit to the plus press of the lift attendant.

beats.on_screen: small title card From your book; a bank counter; a savings of 100 rupees goes into a new account; the next day 60 rupees more go in; the words How much is in the account now? appear

marks.open: 100 rupees go into a new bank account

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book, about a bank account.
<bookmark mark='open'/>You open an account with one hundred rupees that you saved.
<bookmark mark='next'/>The next day you earn sixty rupees at your job and put it in the account.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>How much money is in the account now?

beats.on_screen: the bank account and the question stay on the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

beats.on_screen: a bank passbook page; the words balance and credit are written beside the money in the account and the money put in

marks.balance: the money in the account is boxed and labelled balance
marks.passbook: a passbook page opens with a row for each change
marks.credit: money put in is written in the passbook and labelled credit

narration: <bookmark mark='balance'/>The money in a bank account is called the balance.
<bookmark mark='passbook'/>The bank writes every change to the account in a passbook.
<bookmark mark='credit'/>Money put into the account is called a credit.

beats.on_screen: Given: starting balance ₹100; credit ₹60 the next day

marks.given: the starting balance and the credit are written in two lines

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, the balance starts at one hundred rupees. The next day a credit of sixty rupees goes in.

marks.find: the words the new balance are written and underlined

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the new balance in the account.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: a credit is money put in, so it is positive: credit ₹60 is +60

marks.sign: the credit of ₹60 is written as +60 with an arrow pointing up

narration: <bookmark mark='sign'/>Step one, a credit is money put in, so it takes the balance up. We write it as positive sixty.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: add the credit to the starting balance, 100 + 60

narration: <bookmark mark='add'/>Step two, add the credit to the starting balance.
<bookmark mark='total'/>One hundred rupees and sixty rupees together make one hundred and sixty rupees.

marks.ans: the new balance ₹160 is written and boxed

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>The new balance is one hundred and sixty rupees.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the passbook
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us see where else we meet this idea.

beats.on_screen: the lift attendant from the book beside the passbook; a plus press takes the lift up one floor while a credit takes the balance up

marks.lift: the lift attendant presses plus and the lift goes up one floor
marks.credit: a credit is written in the passbook and the balance goes up in the same way

narration: <bookmark mark='lift'/>In your book, the lift attendant presses plus to go up a floor.
<bookmark mark='credit'/>A credit works in the same way, because it takes the balance up.
<bookmark mark='sign'/>That is why a credit is thought of as a positive number.
